findings.summary: The new rows and javadoc state that InProcessTransport is "the ONLY implementation in the tree" / "the only SequencerTransport in the tree", and a one-command check disproves the quantifier: RemoteSequencerTest defines two further implementations, so the claim only holds if it is read as "the only one outside a test", which is not what it says.
findings.failure_scenario: Someone taking M5.6e, or a reviewer checking the row that justifies it, runs `grep -rn SequencerTransport --include=*.java` and finds three implementations of the interface: sequencer/src/testFixtures/.../InProcessTransport.java:25, and `new SequencerTransport() { ... }` at sequencer/src/test/java/binjava/sequencer/RemoteSequencerTest.java:134 and :207. The row's stated premise is then false as written and the reader cannot tell whether it is stale (someone added a transport since) or merely imprecise (test doubles were meant to be excluded) -- the same class of checkable-and-wrong completeness claim this file has already been through in rounds 3, 4 and 5, and it is now also in production javadoc. The load-bearing claim -- no PRODUCTION implementation -- is true and would survive the wording "the only implementation outside a test".

findings.summary: The M5.6e row assigns the correction of five statements it declares false to M5.20, whose own row reads only "M5's `VERIFIED.md` and the milestone review" and mentions no spec or roadmap correction -- the same overstatement of ownership the same cell condemns four clauses later for M2.1.
findings.failure_scenario: M5.20 is executed as its row and the milestone-review skill read: git log plus SPEC.md are read, findings become rows for the NEXT milestone ("not retrofitted into this one"), and VERIFIED.md is written. scripts/check-milestone-verified.sh forces an evidence line per numbered criterion, so criterion 1 gets an honest OBSERVED-NOT -- but it parses only the `## Acceptance criteria` list, so SPEC.md:5 ("THIS MILESTONE MAKES A MULTI-POD DEPLOYMENT CORRECT FOR THE FIRST TIME"), SPEC.md:11, SPEC.md:377 ("M5.6 | ... the correctness hole closes here") and roadmap.md:14 ("leaves a multi-pod deployment incorrect until this lands") are untouched by any gate and survive M5 being marked complete. A reader planning M6 from the roadmap then reads a completed M5 whose row says multi-pod is now correct. sdd.md rule 8 says a wrong spec is amended, and this tree's own precedent for that is a row of its own -- M5.0 ("the roadmap row corrected to name commit forwarding") and M5.21 ("Correct where three requirements live") -- not a clause inside an unrelated row.

findings.summary: M5.6e is recorded as "todo, owned by M8" and "recorded here so it stops being unowned", but roadmap.md's M8 row -- which is where this tree records every other reassignment into M8 -- says nothing about a production SequencerTransport or ADR-0012's RPC, so the only record of M8's ownership is a cell inside M5's table.
findings.failure_scenario: M8 is decomposed from roadmap.md:17, the document AGENTS.md describes as "milestones in execution order, each with a completion condition". That row enumerates the chaos matrix, the `EndpointSlice` watch/NFR-9 and the degraded `ctl/inbox/` path -- both reassignments having been written INTO the row by M5.21's mechanism -- and names no transport, so M8's SPEC is written without one and the production `SequencerTransport` is unowned again, which is precisely the outcome the row exists to prevent and the same shape as M1.11b, still `todo` from M1. ADR-0012 itself never names a milestone, so it cannot supply the ownership either.
